p.t: The more risk averse have utilities that are more concave: u → ϕ•u with ϕ concave and strictly increasing (Pratt, 1964). The strongly more risk averse have (rescaled) utilities that are additively more concave: u → ϕ • u with λuϕ • u convex and strictly increasing for some λ > 0 (Ross, 1981). The more prudent have utilities whose slopes are more convex: u → ϕ • u with ϕ ′ convex and strictly increasing (Kimball, 1990). What transformations of returns make an investor in the growthoptimal portfolio problem (Kelly, 1956) apparently more risk averse? To elaborate, I consider an investor who maximizes expected log growth à la Kelly (1956). 1 For a safe gross return s > 0 and a risky gross return R > 0, the one-safe-one-risky growth problem is, letting α denote the risky share, max α∈ [0,1] E log((1α)s + αR). A transformation f : (0, ∞) → (0, ∞) sends every asset payoff r to f (r), so that the transformed problem is max α∈ [0,1] E log((1α)f (s) + αf (R)). I interpret Yaari (1969)'s behavioral definition of comparative risk aversion as saying that a more risk-averse investor would always have a lower risky share. My question is: which transformations make the Kelly investor universally more conservative in this manner, for every risk-free return and every finite risky-return distribution?

Ordinary concavity is not enough. We need the new utility to be sufficiently more concave. Finally, motivated by Curello et al. (2025), I study ex-post outside options: after an inside asset pays r, the investor can instead take an outside option b (which is the realization of an ex-ante random variable B). I show that, under a mild support condition, such outside options always make the investor weakly more willing to hold the risky asset. The same conclusion holds in the rational-inattention version, raising the probability of the risky action. An example of a transformation that robustly raises safe demand is f (r) = r/(1+ r). f is increasing and concave, while r/f (r) = 1 + r is affine, hence, convex. A transformation that robustly raises risky demand is f (r) = r + c with c > 0. f is increasing and affine, hence, convex, while r/f (r) = r/(r + c) is concave. To see that mere concavity of the transformation is not enough, let s = 1 and let the risky return be R = 1/2 or R = 4 with equal probabilities. The original risky share is 5/6. The transformation f (r) = √ r is concave, but r/f (r) = √ r is concave, not convex. After transformation, the relative risky returns are √ 1/2 and 2, and the optimum is 1, i.e., the safe share falls.

Classical comparative risk aversion transforms Bernoulli utilities: the more riskaverse utility is an increasing concave transformation of the less risk-averse one. Stronger orders ask for robustness to richer comparisons, such as partial insurance and background risk. Prudence moves the transformation logic to marginal utility. I move the transformation elsewhere: which return scales make the same Kelly investor behave more conservatively in every one-safe-one-risky growth problem? I show that return transformations are not utility transformations in disguise.
